To see why multiplying the conditional survival factors estimates marginal
survival, write the ordered distinct exit times as
$y_1 < y_2 < \cdots < y_m$.
Here $Y$ denotes exit time
(either event time or censoring time),
while $T$ denotes the underlying event time,
which is not always observed.

Because $y_{j-1}$ and $y_j$ are consecutive distinct exit times,
there are no exits between them.
Therefore the conditional probability of surviving between these two
times is 1:

$$
\Pr(Y \geq y_j \mid Y > y_{j-1}) = 1.
$$

Then the event $\{Y \geq y_j\}$ is contained in the event
$\{Y > y_{j-1}\}$, because $y_j > y_{j-1}$. Therefore intersecting
$\{Y \geq y_j\}$ with $\{Y > y_{j-1}\}$ does not change the event:

:::{#thm-km-gaps}
#### Consecutive Exit-Time Identity

If $\Pr(Y \geq y_j \mid Y > y_{j-1}) = 1$, then:

$$\Pr(Y \geq y_j) = \Pr(Y > y_{j-1})$$
:::

:::{.proof}

$$
\ba
\Pr(Y \geq y_j)
\\
&= \Pr(Y \geq y_j, Y > y_{j-1})
\\
&= \Pr(Y \geq y_j \mid Y > y_{j-1}) \Pr(Y > y_{j-1})
\\
&= 1 \Pr(Y > y_{j-1})
\\
&= \Pr(Y > y_{j-1})
\ea
$$
:::

The first equality uses the containment
$\{Y \geq y_j\} \subseteq \{Y > y_{j-1}\}$ ([subset property](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/probability-basics.html#thm-prob-subset)). The second equality uses the
multiplication rule for probabilities, and the third equality uses the
between-exit-time survival assumption.

Let
$\cs(y_j) = \Pr(Y > y_j \mid Y \geq y_j)$
denote the conditional probability of surviving past the exit time $y_j$,
given survival up to $y_j$.
By @thm-km-gaps, the conditioning event $\{Y \geq y_j\}$ has the same
probability as $\{Y > y_{j-1}\}$, so $\cs(y_j)$ is really a conditional
survival probability spanning the previous exit time to this one;
applying @lem-cond-surv-ratio to that pair of times gives:

$$
\ba
\cs(y_j)
&\eqdef \Pr(Y > y_j \mid Y \geq y_j)
&& \text{(definition of } \cs(y_j)\text{)}
\\
&= \frac{\Pr(Y > y_j,\ Y \geq y_j)}{\Pr(Y \geq y_j)}
&& \text{(definition of conditional probability)}
\\
&= \frac{\Pr(Y > y_j)}{\Pr(Y \geq y_j)}
&& \text{(}\{Y > y_j\} \subseteq \{Y \geq y_j\}\text{)}
\\
&= \frac{\Pr(Y > y_j)}{\Pr(Y > y_{j-1})}
&& \text{(consecutive exit-time identity)}
\\
&= \frac{\Pr(Y > y_j,\ Y > y_{j-1})}{\Pr(Y > y_{j-1})}
&& \text{(}\{Y > y_j\} \subseteq \{Y > y_{j-1}\}\text{)}
\\
&= \Pr(Y > y_j \mid Y > y_{j-1})
&& \text{(definition of conditional probability)}
\\
&= \frac{\survf{y_j}}{\survf{y_{j-1}}} ,
&& \text{(conditional survival ratio)}
\ea
$$

so, rearranging, the marginal survival through $y_j$ is written recursively:

$$
\survf{y_j} = \cs(y_j)\,\survf{y_{j-1}}.
$$

The same recursion can be applied repeatedly. If
$S_j = \Pr(Y > y_j)$ and $S_0 = 1$, then:

$$
\ba
S_1
&= \cs(y_1)S_0\\
&= \cs(y_1),\\
S_2
&= \cs(y_2)S_1\\
&= \cs(y_2)\cs(y_1),\\
S_3
&= \cs(y_3)S_2\\
&= \cs(y_3)\cs(y_2)\cs(y_1).
\ea
$$

Continuing in this way gives
$S_j = \prod_{k=1}^j \cs(y_k)$.

To estimate the survival function for the underlying event time $T$,
we replace the conditional survival probabilities $\Pr(T > y_k \mid T \geq y_k)$
with their empirical estimates at the observed exit times.
Substituting these empirical estimates into the product representation gives the Kaplan-Meier product-limit estimator:

$$
\ba
\hat{\Pr}(T > t)
&= \hskmf{t}\\
&= \prod_{k:\, y_k \leq t} \hat{\Pr}(T > y_k \mid T \geq y_k)\\
&= \prod_{k:\, y_k \leq t} \hat{\cs}_k\\
&= \prod_{k:\, y_k \leq t} \frac{r_k - d_k}{r_k}
\ea
$$

where $r_k$ is the number at risk at time $y_k$
and $d_k$ is the number of events (not total exits) at time $y_k$.
The empirical factor $(r_k - d_k)/r_k$ estimates $\Pr(T > y_k \mid T \geq y_k)$
by counting only events in the numerator,
since censoring times do not provide information about the event time distribution.

For any time $t$ between two consecutive exit times, the estimate stays
constant, because the only additional conditional survival factors are 1.
